title: Other religions (Nostra Aetate, 1965)
hook: the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions

segments.voice: Yesterday, ecumenism: the search for unity among Christians. Your line was that they may be one. Who did you say something kind about? Today, a wider circle: the Church and people of other religions. Day three hundred twenty-one.

Athens, the first century. Paul walks through the city and sees altars everywhere, and one with an inscription: to the unknown god. He's invited to speak on the Areopagus, a hill where the city's thinkers gathered. He doesn't start by mocking their altars. He starts by quoting their own poets. "For in him we live, and move, and are," he says, and adds that some of their poets had said we are God's offspring. Nineteen centuries later, the Catholic Church wrote a short document about people of other religions, and its tone sounds a lot like Paul on that hill.
screen: `ATHENS: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` → `PAUL QUOTES THEIR POETS.` → `NINETEEN CENTURIES LATER.`

segments.voice: First, the document. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council issued a declaration named, like most Church documents, by its first Latin words: Nostra Aetate, in our age. It's one of the shortest documents of the council. Second, its central sentence. The council says the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions. It speaks with sincere respect of their ways of living and acting, their teachings, and says they often reflect a ray of the truth that enlightens all people. It names Hindus and Buddhists and their searching, and speaks with esteem of Muslims, who worship the one God and honor Abraham, Jesus as a prophet, and Mary. The same document says the Church also keeps proclaiming Christ, and holds both together. Third, the Jewish people. The longest section is about Jews. It speaks of the spiritual heritage Christians share with them. It says that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time, or against Jews today. And it deplores hatred and antisemitism at any time and from any source. Given the centuries before, many historians count it among the council's most important paragraphs. Fourth, what followed. In 1986 Pope John Paul II invited leaders of many religions to Assisi to pray for peace, each in their own way, side by side. The Church asks Catholics to meet their neighbors of other faiths with respect, to learn, and to work together for the good. Nothing true is rejected. Not because every belief is the same, but because truth, wherever it's found, is taken seriously.
screen: `NOSTRA AETATE: IN OUR AGE.` · `NOTHING TRUE AND HOLY REJECTED.` · `NO COLLECTIVE BLAME ON THE JEWS.` · `ASSISI, 1986: SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `NOTHING TRUE IS REJECTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one prayer from another tradition. Not to pray it as your own, but to hear it as a guest. Settle, and breathe. Here is one Jews say every morning and evening, from Deuteronomy: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Let it sound in you, slowly. Think of the people who say it tonight before they sleep. If you know someone of another faith, think of them too, and of the words they pray. Hold them with respect. The bell holds the time.
Other religions. How the Catholic Church, since Nostra Aetate in 1965, speaks of other faiths: with respect, rejecting nothing true and holy in them. Today's word.
Your line: nothing true is rejected. Today, ask someone of another faith, or look up, one thing their tradition holds dear, and listen. Day three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic dioceses run interreligious dialogue offices, parishes share service projects and study with neighboring synagogues, mosques and temples, and popes have met leaders of other religions, as at Assisi in 1986.

fork.reveal: Paul starts from what they already know and love: for in him we live, and move, and are.

original.note: Latin: in our age, the first words and name of the 1965 declaration.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Church thinks other religions are simply wrong.
what it means: the Church rejects nothing true and holy in them, speaks of them with respect, and still proclaims Christ.
what a scholar hears: Nostra Aetate 2 and 4; Acts 17:22–31; the rejection of collective Jewish guilt; the 1986 Assisi Day of Prayer.
